title: Review: Enthalpy change, exo/endothermic and profiles; Collision theory and factors
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EN01#t1 term and clue written for the game; KN02#t3 term and clue written for the game; EN01#t4 term and clue written for the game; KN02#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EN01#N.4a, KN02#N.2a, EN01#N.7a, KN02#N.7a, EN01#N.11a, KN02#N.4a, EN01#N.13, KN02#N.9b. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: System
items.clue: The reacting chemicals themselves: the reactants and the products.

items.label: Catalyst
items.clue: Provides an alternative route with a lower Ea, leaving ΔH unchanged.

items.label: Activation energy
items.clue: The minimum needed for reaction: from the reactant level to the top of the hump.

items.label: Collision theory
items.clue: The idea that particles must hit each other, with enough energy, in order to react.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the temperature of a substance?

options.text: The form of energy that flows from a hot object to a cold one
A measure of the total kinetic energy of all the particles it has
A quantity that has to rise whenever heat is transferred into it
A measure of the average kinetic energy of its particles

questions.explanation: Temperature is an average over the particles. It does not depend on how many there are, and it is not itself energy that is transferred.

questions.stem: In a mixture of two gases at room temperature, each molecule collides with others billions of times every second, yet the reaction between them is slow. Why do most of these collisions not lead to a reaction?

options.text: Most collisions have less energy than ΔH, the energy that the reaction gives out.
Most collisions have less energy than Ea, the minimum needed for a reaction.
A catalyst must be present in each collision before any bonds can break.
Most of the molecules are moving far too slowly to collide with one another.

questions.explanation: Only collisions with energy of at least Ea lead to reaction. At room temperature that is a tiny fraction, so the reaction is slow.

questions.stem: A mixture of iron and sulfur must be heated strongly before it reacts. Once started, it glows red-hot with no further heating. What does this show?

options.text: The reaction is endothermic, because it needs heating to start.
The reaction is endothermic at first, then becomes exothermic once it starts.
The reaction is exothermic; the heating just gets it started.
Neither: the glow is the heat supplied at the start being given back.

questions.explanation: Most reactions need energy to get started, the activation energy. This one then releases more energy than it took in, so it keeps itself going: exothermic.

questions.stem: Which statement explains how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction at constant temperature?

options.text: It gives the reacting particles more kinetic energy, so more collisions exceed Ea.
It increases the concentration of the reactants, so collisions happen more often.
It makes the reaction more exothermic, so more energy is available for collisions.
It provides a route with a lower Ea, so a larger fraction of collisions have enough energy.

questions.explanation: Same particles, same energies, but a lower barrier. More collisions now have E ≥ Ea, so more succeed each second.

questions.stem: An enthalpy profile for a reaction shows, relative to the same zero, the reactants at 150 kJ mol⁻¹, the top of the energy barrier at 280 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products at 40 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.text: −110 kJ mol⁻¹
+110 kJ mol⁻¹
+130 kJ mol⁻¹
−240 kJ mol⁻¹

questions.explanation: ΔH = products − reactants = 40 − 150 = −110 kJ mol⁻¹. Products below reactants: exothermic.

questions.stem: Hydrogen iodide decomposes: 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g). A sample of hydrogen iodide is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. What is the effect on the rate of reaction, and why?

options.text: It is unchanged: there are equal amounts of gas on both sides of the equation, so pressure has no effect.
It increases: the compressed molecules collide more energetically, so more collisions exceed Ea.
It increases: a larger amount of H₂ and I₂ can now form from the same amount of HI as before.
It increases: collisions become more frequent, and the fraction with E ≥ Ea is unchanged.

questions.stem: Hydrated barium hydroxide and ammonium chloride, both solids, are mixed in a flask standing on a wet wooden block. Within a minute the water under the flask freezes, sticking the flask to the block. Which statement about the reacting chemicals is correct?

options.text: They lose energy to the water, which then freezes; ΔH is negative.
They release "cold", which spreads into the water and freezes it; ΔH is positive.
Energy is used up as the solids react, so the water freezes; ΔH is negative.
They gain energy from the water, flask and air; ΔH is positive.

questions.explanation: The surroundings cool because energy flows into the system. The system gains energy: endothermic, ΔH positive.

questions.stem: A glowing splint only smoulders in air, but bursts into flame when it is lowered into a gas jar of pure oxygen at the same temperature and pressure. Air is about 21% oxygen. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Molecules of pure oxygen have more kinetic energy, so their collisions with the wood are more energetic.
Each unit volume holds about five times as many O₂ molecules, so collisions with the wood are far more frequent.
Pure oxygen acts as a catalyst, giving a route with a lower activation energy for the burning of wood.
Pure oxygen contains no nitrogen, so each mole of O₂ that reacts with the wood releases more energy.
